stories.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression ," wrote the signatories of the appeal. The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English. The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times. As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower. Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died. Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened. stories.article_text_excerpt: Cancer claims 10 million lives each year, the global shortage of health workers runs into the millions, and in some parts of the world, a single mosquito bite can be fatal. These challenges may seem very different. Yet they share a common element in how many health systems operate: risk is often recognised only after it has become illness, outbreak or crisis. By then, a disease may have advanced, transmission of disease may be under way, or an already stretched workforce may be managing consequences that earlier action could have reduced. The opportunity is to move that point of intervention earlier. This is what anticipatory health means in practice: using signals that already exist, at the bedside, in communities, and in routine health data, to help people and health systems act sooner. It is not prediction for its own sake. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response. stories.article_text_excerpt: With 0.56% support, Te Pāti Māori will be stoked with its result tonight, writes Jamie Tahana. It seems odd, but the Māori party has spent the election deliberately asking people not to give them their party vote. Instead, they asked for electorate votes only. Just a reminder, seven of the seats in New Zealand’s parliament are reserved for representatives of Māori voters – you can read more about them here. The party’s co-leaders, Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, have comfortably won their respective seats of Waiariki and Te Tai Hauauru; Oriini Kaipara swept the Auckland seat of Tamaki Makaurau; Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who hit international stardom for her haka in parliament, has cruised across the line in Hauraki-Waikato; while Aperahama Edwards holds a narrow lead over the Greens’ Hūhana Lydon in the far North seat of Te Tai Tokerau. stories.summary: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

stories.title: Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability
stories.summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

stories.title: Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia
stories.summary: International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

stories.title: Son of Iran's shah receives 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt
stories.summary: 18,000 people gathered in Frankfurt to show support for Reza Pahlavi, the son of the Iranian monarch ousted in 1979. Factions in the opposition have accused him of not distancing himself from his father's rule.

stories.title: Armenia's selective prosecution: A threat to EU relations?
stories.summary: While Brussels has refrained from harsh criticism, Armenian civil society has warned of selective justice against opposition figures. Could the EU's pragmatic stance risk repeating past mistakes?

stories.summary: European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

stories.title: What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship
